reference.source: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
clinicalPearls: An infection of the pneumatised petrous apex, usually a complication of acute or chronic otitis media and mastoiditis
The classic Gradenigo triad comprises otorrhoea, deep retro-orbital or facial pain in the trigeminal distribution, and an abducens (sixth nerve) palsy causing horizontal diplopia
The triad reflects spread of infection to the petrous apex, involving the trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion and the abducens nerve in Dorello canal
It has become uncommon in the antibiotic era but remains an important cause of cranial neuropathy complicating ear infection
The full triad is often incomplete, so persistent otorrhoea with new headache or diplopia should raise suspicion
Contrast CT and MRI of the temporal bone demonstrate petrous apex opacification, bony erosion and any associated intracranial complication
Management centres on culture-directed antimicrobial therapy with drainage of the middle ear and mastoid, and surgical drainage of the petrous apex in refractory or complicated cases
Meningitis, intracranial abscess, and dural venous sinus thrombosis are feared complications requiring urgent recognition
reference.pathophysiology: The petrous apex is variably pneumatised and connected to the middle ear and mastoid air-cell system. Infection of the middle ear and mastoid can extend into these apical air cells, and if drainage is impaired the trapped infection progresses to osteomyelitis of the petrous apex. Its anatomical relations explain the syndrome: inflammation irritates the trigeminal ganglion at the petrous apex causing facial pain, and involves the abducens nerve as it passes through Dorello canal beneath the petroclinoid ligament, producing a lateral rectus palsy. Further spread can breach the dura, leading to meningitis, intracranial abscess or venous sinus thrombosis.
additionalDifferentials: Uncomplicated acute otitis media or mastoiditis
Petrous apex cholesteatoma or cholesterol granuloma
Skull-base osteomyelitis, including necrotising (malignant) otitis externa
Nasopharyngeal or skull-base tumour involving the petrous apex
Cavernous sinus or dural venous sinus thrombosis of other cause
Trigeminal neuralgia or other cause of isolated abducens palsy
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the temporal bone to show petrous apex opacification and bony erosion
MRI with contrast to assess soft-tissue and intracranial extension
Microbiological culture of ear discharge or intraoperative samples
Inflammatory markers and blood cultures to gauge systemic infection
Lumbar puncture where meningitis is suspected and safe to perform after imaging
redFlags: Signs of meningitis such as neck stiffness, photophobia and altered consciousness
New or multiple cranial nerve palsies indicating skull-base spread
Features of intracranial abscess or dural venous sinus thrombosis
High fever and systemic toxicity suggesting severe or complicated infection
reference.prognosis: With prompt culture-directed antimicrobial therapy and appropriate drainage, most cases resolve and the abducens palsy often recovers, though recovery can be slow. Delayed treatment risks serious intracranial complications with significant morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Attributing persistent otorrhoea with headache to simple otitis media and missing evolving petrous apicitis
Overlooking an incomplete Gradenigo triad, since all three features are frequently not present together
Failing to image the intracranial compartment when new cranial nerve signs appear
Inadequate drainage of the petrous apex or mastoid, allowing infection to persist or progress
